claim: SARS-CoV-2 was measured for stability on polypropylene at nine temperature and humidity conditions.
source: We measured the environmental stability of SARS-CoV-2 virus particles (virions) suspended in cell culture medium and deposited onto a polypropylene plastic surface at nine environmental conditions: three relative humidities (RH; 40%, 65%, and 85%) at each of three temperatures (10°C, 22°C, and 27°C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design and conditions tested.

claim: The median estimated virus half-life of SARS-CoV-2 is greater than 24 hours at 10°C and 40% RH.
source: We find SARS-CoV-2 survives longest at low temperatures and extreme relative humidities (RH); median estimated virus half-life is >24 hr at 10°C and 40% RH, but ∼1.5 hr at 27°C and 65% RH.
evidence: The abstract reports measured half-life values from the experimental data.

claim: The median estimated virus half-life of SARS-CoV-2 is approximately 1.5 hours at 27°C and 65% RH.
source: We find SARS-CoV-2 survives longest at low temperatures and extreme relative humidities (RH); median estimated virus half-life is >24 hr at 10°C and 40% RH, but ∼1.5 hr at 27°C and 65% RH.
evidence: The abstract reports measured half-life values from the experimental data.

claim: Virus inactivation rate increases with increased temperature.
source: Our mechanistic model uses fundamental chemistry to explain why inactivation rate increases with increased temperature and shows a U-shaped dependence on RH.
evidence: The abstract describes findings from the mechanistic model based on experimental data.

claim: Virus inactivation rate shows a U-shaped dependence on relative humidity.
source: Our mechanistic model uses fundamental chemistry to explain why inactivation rate increases with increased temperature and shows a U-shaped dependence on RH.
evidence: The abstract describes findings from the mechanistic model based on experimental data.

claim: The mechanistic model accurately predicts existing measurements of five different human coronaviruses.
source: The model accurately predicts existing measurements of five different human coronaviruses, suggesting that shared mechanisms may affect stability for many viruses.
evidence: The abstract reports the model's predictive performance on independent data.

claim: Shared mechanisms may affect stability for many viruses.
source: The model accurately predicts existing measurements of five different human coronaviruses, suggesting that shared mechanisms may affect stability for many viruses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model's ability to predict multiple virus species.

claim: Ambient temperature and humidity strongly affect inactivation rates of enveloped viruses.
source: Ambient temperature and humidity strongly affect inactivation rates of enveloped viruses, but a mechanistic, quantitative theory of these effects has been elusive.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Virus environmental stability depends strongly on ambient temperature and humidity, particularly for enveloped viruses.
source: Empirical evidence suggests that virus environmental stability depends strongly on ambient temperature and humidity, particularly for enveloped viruses; examples among enveloped viruses that infect humans include influenza viruses (Marr et al., 2019), endemic human coronaviruses (Ijaz et al., 1985), and the zoonotic coronaviruses SARS-CoV-1 (Chan et al., 2011) and MERS-CoV (van Doremalen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 emerged in late 2019 and has caused a global pandemic.
source: In late 2019, a new zoonotic coronavirus now called SARS-CoV-2 emerged; it has since caused a global pandemic (COVID-19) and is poised to become an endemic human pathogen.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the COVID-19 pandemic.

claim: Many countries in the Northern Hemisphere experienced a substantial uptick in SARS-CoV-2 transmission with the arrival of late autumn and winter.
source: Many countries in the Northern Hemisphere experienced a substantial uptick in transmission with the arrival of their late autumn and winter.
evidence: This is stated as an observed epidemiological pattern.

claim: Epidemiologists had anticipated a seasonal increase in SARS-CoV-2 transmission based on observations from other enveloped respiratory viruses.
source: Epidemiologists had anticipated such a seasonal increase (Neher et al., 2020; Kissler et al., 2020) based on observations from other enveloped respiratory viruses, such as endemic human coronaviruses (Monto et al., 2020) and influenza viruses (Lofgren et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Endemic human coronaviruses and influenza viruses spread more readily in temperate zone winters than in temperate zone summers.
source: Epidemiologists had anticipated such a seasonal increase (Neher et al., 2020; Kissler et al., 2020) based on observations from other enveloped respiratory viruses, such as endemic human coronaviruses (Monto et al., 2020) and influenza viruses (Lofgren et al., 2007). These viruses spread more readily in temperate zone winters than in temperate zone summers.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has displayed epidemic dynamics shaped by superspreading events.
source: SARS-CoV-2 has also displayed epidemic dynamics shaped by superspreading events, in which one person transmits to many others (Furuse et al., 2020; Kain et al., 2021); the related SARS-CoV-1 virus was likewise characterized by superspreading (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-1 was characterized by superspreading.
source: SARS-CoV-2 has also displayed epidemic dynamics shaped by superspreading events, in which one person transmits to many others (Furuse et al., 2020; Kain et al., 2021); the related SARS-CoV-1 virus was likewise characterized by superspreading (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 varies in its environmental stability as a function of temperature and humidity.
source: Empirical evidence suggests that SARS-CoV-2, like other enveloped viruses, varies in its environmental stability as a function of temperature and humidity (Biryukov et al., 2020; Matson et al., 2020), but the joint effect of these two factors remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There do not exist mechanistically motivated quantitative models for virus inactivation as a function of both temperature and humidity.
source: Moreover, despite years of research on virus environmental stability, there do not exist mechanistically motivated quantitative models for virus inactivation as a function of both temperature and humidity.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the existing literature.

claim: Existing predictive models for the environmental stability of SARS-CoV-2 and other viruses are phenomenological regression models that do not model the underlying biochemical mechanisms of inactivation.
source: Existing predictive models for the environmental stability of SARS-CoV-2 (Biryukov et al., 2020; Guillier et al., 2020) and other viruses (Posada et al., 2010) are phenomenological regression models that do not model the underlying biochemical mechanisms of inactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Posterior median estimated virus half-life is 27 hours [20, 39] at 10°C and 40% RH once droplets reach quasi-equilibrium.
source: Our data suggest that SARS-CoV-2 environmental persistence could vary meaningfully across the range of temperatures and humidities encountered in daily life, with posterior median [95% credible interval] half-lives as long as 27 hr [20, 39] (10°C, 40% RH) and as short as 1.5 hr [1.1, 2.1] (27°C, 65% RH), once droplets reach quasi-equilibrium with the ambient air conditions (Figure 1b, Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements.

claim: Posterior median estimated virus half-life is 1.5 hours [1.1, 2.1] at 27°C and 65% RH once droplets reach quasi-equilibrium.
source: Our data suggest that SARS-CoV-2 environmental persistence could vary meaningfully across the range of temperatures and humidities encountered in daily life, with posterior median [95% credible interval] half-lives as long as 27 hr [20, 39] (10°C, 40% RH) and as short as 1.5 hr [1.1, 2.1] (27°C, 65% RH), once droplets reach quasi-equilibrium with the ambient air conditions (Figure 1b, Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements.

claim: Minimal virus decay occurred during the evaporation phase when excess water was present.
source: Minimal virus decay occurred during the evaporation phase (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), when excess water was present.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Posterior median half-lives during the evaporation phase were 42 hr [11, 330] at 10°C.
source: Posterior median half-lives during the evaporation phase were 42 hr [11, 330] at 10°C, 12 hr [4.5, 160] at 22°C, and 5.8 hr [2.1, 130] at 27°C (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements.

claim: Posterior median half-lives during the evaporation phase were 12 hr [4.5, 160] at 22°C.
source: Posterior median half-lives during the evaporation phase were 42 hr [11, 330] at 10°C, 12 hr [4.5, 160] at 22°C, and 5.8 hr [2.1, 130] at 27°C (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements.

claim: Posterior median half-lives during the evaporation phase were 5.8 hr [2.1, 130] at 27°C.
source: Posterior median half-lives during the evaporation phase were 42 hr [11, 330] at 10°C, 12 hr [4.5, 160] at 22°C, and 5.8 hr [2.1, 130] at 27°C (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements.

claim: Virus decay became markedly faster as temperature increased for all humidities, with decay at 27°C roughly five to ten times faster than decay at 10°C.
source: Overall, virus decay became markedly faster as temperature increased for all humidities, with decay at 27°C roughly five to ten times faster than decay at 10°C.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Virus decay was relatively rapid at 65% RH and tended to be slower either at lower (40%) or higher (85%) humidities.
source: Across temperatures, virus decay was relatively rapid at 65% RH and tended to be slower either at lower (40%) or higher (85%) humidities, or when excess water was present during the evaporation phase (Figure 1b, Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in figures and tables.

claim: Many viruses, including SARS-CoV-2, exhibit exponential decay on surfaces and in aerosols.
source: Many viruses, including SARS-CoV-2, exhibit exponential decay on surfaces and in aerosols (Marr et al., 2019; van Doremalen et al., 2020; Biryukov et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Virus inactivation at quasi-equilibrium on inert surfaces is modeled as a chemical reaction with first-order reaction kinetics.
source: We model virus inactivation at quasi-equilibrium on inert surfaces as a chemical reaction with first-order reaction kinetics; that is, the quantity of virus is the limiting reactant of the rate-determining step.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on empirical patterns.

claim: Prior work has found Arrhenius-like temperature dependence for virus inactivation on surfaces and in aerosols for many viruses, including human coronaviruses.
source: Prior work has found Arrhenius-like temperature dependence for virus inactivation on surfaces and in aerosols for many viruses (Adams, 1949), including human coronaviruses (Yap et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Relative humidity affects virus inactivation by controlling evaporation and thus governing the solute concentrations in a droplet containing virions.
source: Recent work has suggested that relative humidity affects virus inactivation by controlling evaporation and thus governing the solute concentrations in a droplet containing virions (Marr et al., 2019; Lin and Marr, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Higher quasi-equilibrium solute concentrations are associated with faster virus inactivation rates.
source: Prior work has found that higher quasi-equilibrium solute concentrations are associated with faster virus inactivation rates (Yang and Marr, 2012; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Below a threshold ambient humidity—the efflorescence relative humidity (ERH)—electrolytes effloresce out of solution, forming a crystal.
source: Below a threshold ambient humidity—the efflorescence relative humidity (ERH)—electrolytes effloresce out of solution, forming a crystal (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated as a known chemical principle and illustrated in a figure.

claim: The non-monotonic ('U-shaped') dependence of virus inactivation on relative humidity has been observed for coronaviruses.
source: The non-monotonic ('U-shaped') dependence of virus inactivation on relative humidity, observed in our data (Figure 1a) and elsewhere in the literature (Yang et al., 2012; Benbough, 1971; Prussin et al., 2018; Webb et al., 1963), including for coronaviruses (Casanova et al., 2010; Songer, 1967), could be explained by this regime shift around the ERH (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and the current study's data.

claim: An efflorescence relative humidity (ERH) of 45% is used in the model based on observations of NaCl solutions at room temperature and atmospheric pressure.
source: Based on observations of NaCl solutions at room temperature and atmospheric pressure (Mikhailov et al., 2004), we use an ERH of 45%.
evidence: This is a modeling parameter choice based on cited literature.

claim: The fit of the mechanistic model is nearly as good as that of the simple regression, in which independent exponential decay rates are estimated for each condition.
source: Remarkably, the fit of the mechanistic model (Figure 2) is nearly as good as that of the simple regression, in which we estimate independent exponential decay rates for each condition to measure virus half-life (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, see Appendix, Simple regression model).
evidence: This is a comparison of model performance based on the data.

claim: Median predicted SARS-CoV-2 half-life varies by more than three orders of magnitude, from less than half an hour at 40°C just above the modeled approximate ERH, to more than a month at 0°C and 100% RH.
source: Median predicted SARS-CoV-2 half-life varies by more than three orders of magnitude, from less than half an hour at 40°C just above the modeled approximate ERH, to more than a month at 0°C and 100% RH (Figure 3a,c).
evidence: This is a prediction from the mechanistic model shown in figures.

claim: Striking agreement was found between model predictions and model-free estimates for half-life estimates both above and below the ERH, and for temperatures ranging from 4°C to 37°C.
source: We found striking agreement for half-life estimates both above and below the ERH, and for temperatures ranging from 4°C to 37°C.
evidence: This is a summary of the out-of-sample validation results.

claim: Predicted half-lives matched observations well across five orders of magnitude, spanning five virus species.
source: Predicted half-lives matched observations well across five orders of magnitude (Figure 3d), despite spanning five virus species and despite important heterogeneities in the data collection process (see Appendix, Meta-analysis of human coronavirus half-lives).
evidence: This is a summary of the meta-analysis validation results.

claim: The mechanistic model provides a mechanism for the non-linear and non-monotonic relationship between relative humidity and virus stability previously observed for numerous enveloped viruses.
source: Combining novel data, mathematical modeling, and a meta-analysis of existing literature, we have developed a unified, mechanistic framework to quantify the joint effects of temperature and humidity on virus stability. In particular, our model provides a mechanism for the non-linear and non-monotonic relationship between relative humidity and virus stability previously observed for numerous enveloped viruses (Yang and Marr, 2012; Casanova et al., 2010; Songer, 1967), but not previously reported for SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution, supported by citations.

claim: The work documents and explains the strong dependence of SARS-CoV-2 stability on environmental temperature and relative humidity.
source: Our work documents and explains the strong dependence of SARS-CoV-2 stability on environmental temperature and relative humidity, and accurately predicts half-lives for five coronavirus species in conditions from 4°C to 95°C, and from 30% to 80% RH and in bulk solution.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The model accurately predicts half-lives for five coronavirus species in conditions from 4°C to 95°C, and from 30% to 80% RH and in bulk solution.
source: Our work documents and explains the strong dependence of SARS-CoV-2 stability on environmental temperature and relative humidity, and accurately predicts half-lives for five coronavirus species in conditions from 4°C to 95°C, and from 30% to 80% RH and in bulk solution.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's predictive performance.

claim: The majority of SARS-CoV-2 clusters have been linked to indoor settings.
source: The majority of SARS-CoV-2 clusters have been linked to indoor settings (Leclerc et al., 2020), suggesting that virus stability in indoor environmental conditions may be an important determinant of superspreading risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Virus stability in indoor environmental conditions may be an important determinant of superspreading risk.
source: The majority of SARS-CoV-2 clusters have been linked to indoor settings (Leclerc et al., 2020), suggesting that virus stability in indoor environmental conditions may be an important determinant of superspreading risk.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited observation about indoor clusters.

claim: The results provide a mechanistic explanation for the many observed SARS-CoV-2 superspreading events in cool indoor environments such as food processing plants and hockey rinks.
source: Our results provide a mechanistic explanation for the many observed SARS-CoV-2 superspreading events in cool indoor environments such as food processing plants (Dyal, 2020; Günther et al., 2020; Pokora et al., 2020) and hockey rinks (Atrubin et al., 2020; McNabb and Ries, 2020), where the typical air temperature is around 10°C, or in dry indoor environments such as long-distance flights (Khanh et al., 2020; Jayaweera et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings applied to cited observations.

claim: The relative rarity of outdoor SARS-CoV-2 transmission clusters is not readily explained by temperature and humidity effects.
source: Conversely, our results imply that the relative rarity of outdoor SARS-CoV-2 transmission clusters is not readily explained by temperature and humidity effects, since these conditions outdoors during temperate zone winters should be favorable for the virus.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings.

claim: Increased ventilation and UV light inactivation may be more important than the effects of temperature and humidity outdoors.
source: Instead, increased ventilation (Prather et al., 2020) and UV light inactivation (Ratnesar-Shumate et al., 2020) may be more important than the effects of temperature and humidity outdoors.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Typical climate-controlled conditions indoors (moderate temperature and low humidity) are favorable for virus stability.
source: In contrast, typical climate-controlled conditions indoors (moderate temperature and low humidity) are favorable for virus stability, and specialized conditions such as those found in food processing plants even more so.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings.

claim: The effects of temperature and humidity observed in the data and model are relevant both to fomite and to airborne transmission.
source: The effects of temperature and humidity we observe in our data and model are relevant both to fomite and to airborne transmission.
evidence: This is an inference about the applicability of the findings.

claim: Virus decay as a function of RH is similar in droplets on surfaces and suspended aerosols.
source: Prior work has shown that virus decay as a function of RH is similar in droplets on surfaces and suspended aerosols (Lin and Marr, 2020; Kormuth et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Numerous studies of smaller deposited droplets or aerosols have reported similar qualitative patterns with increased decay rates at high temperatures and a U-shaped effect of RH.
source: Numerous studies of smaller deposited droplets (Prussin et al., 2018) or aerosols (Benbough, 1971; Yang et al., 2012; Ijaz et al., 1985) have reported similar qualitative patterns to those we report, with increased decay rates at high temperatures and a U-shaped effect of RH.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Small particles containing infectious virions can be re-suspended from surfaces and inhaled.
source: Furthermore, surface stability can matter for aerosol transmission risk, since small particles containing infectious virions can be re-suspended from surfaces and inhaled (Asadi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Re-suspension is enhanced by procedures such as high-pressure washing, which is common in food processing plants.
source: Re-suspension is further enhanced by procedures such as high-pressure washing, which is common in food processing plants.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about food processing practices.

claim: Cold situations present elevated transmission risks for either aerosol or fomite transmission modes.
source: While the relative contributions of aerosol and fomite transmission to the epidemiology of SARS-CoV-2 continue to be investigated (Ong et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2020), our results indicate that cold situations present elevated transmission risks for either mode, especially if air is either dry or very humid.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings.

claim: It has been speculated that chilled or frozen foods might allow for rare but impactful long-range fomite transmission.
source: It has been speculated, for instance, that chilled or frozen foods might allow for rare but impactful long-range fomite transmission (Han et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The results show that long-range fomite transmission via chilled or frozen foods is conceivable, as there is good empirical and mechanistic support for prolonged virus viability at very low temperatures.
source: Our results show that this is conceivable, as there is good empirical and mechanistic support for prolonged virus viability at very low temperatures.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings applied to a speculative scenario.

claim: Environmental stability is not the only mechanism by which temperature and humidity affect respiratory virus transmission.
source: Environmental stability is not the only mechanism by which temperature and humidity affect respiratory virus transmission.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat about the scope of the findings.

claim: Very hot or cold conditions outdoors can lead people to spend more time indoors, where transmission risks are heightened due to poor ventilation.
source: Very hot or cold conditions outdoors can lead people to spend more time indoors, where transmission risks are heightened due to poor ventilation.
evidence: This is stated as a known behavioral and environmental factor.

claim: Low-humidity environments can dry out human airways and thus impair defenses against respiratory viruses.
source: Low-humidity environments can dry out human airways and thus impair defenses against respiratory viruses (Kudo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Ambient humidity determines the size distribution of aerosols in the environment by affecting evaporation rates.
source: Ambient humidity also determines the size distribution of aerosols in the environment, again by affecting evaporation rates.
evidence: This is stated as a known physical principle.

claim: Smaller aerosols settle to the ground more slowly, which could facilitate transmission.
source: Smaller aerosols settle to the ground more slowly (Marr et al., 2019), which could facilitate transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited physical principles.

claim: At low RH, humidity effects on inactivation, immunity, and settling may compound each other to increase transmission risk.
source: At low RH, humidity effects on inactivation, immunity, and settling may compound each other: all increase transmission risk.
evidence: This is an inference about the combined effects of multiple mechanisms.

claim: At high RH, reduced inactivation could promote transmission, but improved immune defenses and faster settling could hinder it, so the net effect on transmission is less clear.
source: At high RH, reduced inactivation could promote transmission, but improved immune defenses and faster settling could hinder it, so the net effect on transmission is less clear.
evidence: This is an inference about the combined effects of multiple mechanisms.

claim: Temperate zone winters increase transmission of many respiratory viruses.
source: Still, temperate zone winters increase transmission of many respiratory viruses (Lofgren et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Individuals spend increased time indoors in heated buildings during temperate zone winters.
source: Individuals spend increased time indoors in heated buildings.
evidence: This is stated as a known behavioral pattern.

claim: Ventilation is often poor in heated buildings during winter, as windows are kept closed to make heating efficient.
source: Ventilation is often poor, as windows are kept closed to make heating efficient.
evidence: This is stated as a known environmental condition.

claim: Air in heated buildings is typically very dry, which improves virus stability and weakens immune defenses.
source: Air in heated buildings is typically very dry; this improves virus stability and weakens immune defenses.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings combined with known environmental conditions.

claim: Several analyses have projected that SARS-CoV-2 transmission will be faster in temperate zone winters.
source: Several analyses have projected that SARS-CoV-2 transmission will likewise be faster in temperate zone winters (Neher et al., 2020; Kissler et al., 2020; Baker et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Major seasonal or climate-mediated mitigation of SARS-CoV-2 spread was not evident during the northern hemisphere's spring and summer.
source: Major seasonal or climate-mediated mitigation of SARS-CoV-2 spread was not evident during the northern hemisphere's spring and summer (Carlson et al., 2020; Poirier et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Population susceptibility and epidemic control measures can be more important than seasonality in an early pandemic context.
source: This was expected, since population susceptibility and epidemic control measures can be more important than seasonality in an early pandemic context (Baker et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Winter surges in cases, hospitalizations, and deaths across the northern hemisphere may have been driven in part by behavioral, immunological, or virological seasonality.
source: Winter surges in cases, hospitalizations, and deaths across the northern hemisphere may have been driven in part by behavioral, immunological, or virological seasonality.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the causes of observed patterns.

claim: Whether absolute or relative humidity is more important for influenza stability has been a matter of debate.
source: Whether absolute or relative humidity is more important for influenza stability has been a matter of debate (Shaman et al., 2010; Marr et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mechanistic model permits principled dis-aggregation of the effects of humidity from those of temperature.
source: The answer has proved elusive because it is difficult to disentangle the effects of humidity from those of temperature. Our mechanistic model permits principled dis-aggregation of those effects, and reveals a strong effect of relative humidity even after accounting for the effects of temperature.
evidence: This is a claim about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The model reveals a strong effect of relative humidity even after accounting for the effects of temperature.
source: Our mechanistic model permits principled dis-aggregation of those effects, and reveals a strong effect of relative humidity even after accounting for the effects of temperature.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: General principles may govern virus inactivation across enveloped viruses, and perhaps even more broadly.
source: There may thus exist general principles that govern virus inactivation across enveloped viruses, and perhaps even more broadly.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the study's findings.

claim: The U-shaped dependence of inactivation on RH has been reported for animal coronaviruses, influenza viruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, and retroviruses.
source: In particular, the U-shaped dependence of inactivation on RH has been reported for animal coronaviruses (Songer, 1967; Casanova et al., 2010), as well as for influenza viruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, and retroviruses (Yang et al., 2012; Benbough, 1971; Prussin et al., 2018; Webb et al., 1963), suggesting the existence of a shared mechanism for the effect of humidity across enveloped RNA viruses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some enveloped DNA viruses such as herpesviruses and poxviruses show similar empirical behavior to the U-shaped humidity dependence.
source: Some enveloped DNA viruses such as herpesviruses and poxviruses (Songer, 1967; Webb et al., 1963) and some encapsulated viruses such as polioviruses (de Jong and Winkler, 1968; Songer, 1967) also show similar empirical behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Experiments have found that heat treatment of viruses reduces infectivity principally by degrading surface proteins.
source: Experiments have found that heat treatment of viruses reduces infectivity principally by degrading surface proteins (Wigginton et al., 2012), lending further support to a chemical model of environmental virus inactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Individual enveloped viruses may be more or less stable than SARS-CoV-2 while still obeying the model's basic principle that increased heat and concentration lead to faster inactivation.
source: Individual enveloped viruses may be more or less stable than SARS-CoV-2 while still obeying our model's basic principle: increased heat and concentration lead to faster inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference about the generalizability of the model.

claim: The model predictions using SARS-CoV-2 parameters slightly overestimate the stability of MERS-CoV, but correctly predict the pattern of temperature and humidity effects.
source: The data from our own group and from the literature on MERS-CoV is suggestive in this regard: our model predictions using SARS-CoV-2 parameters slightly overestimate the stability of MERS-CoV, but correctly predict the pattern of temperature and humidity effects (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions to data.

claim: The model for Arrhenius-like temperature dependence works well with a single estimated activation energy across the effloresced and solution regimes for SARS-CoV-2 experiments and for experiments on a range of coronaviruses conducted by other investigators.
source: Similarly, it is striking that our model for Arrhenius-like temperature dependence works well with a single estimated activation energy across the effloresced and solution regimes for our SARS-CoV-2 experiments and for experiments on a range of coronaviruses conducted in different conditions by other investigators.
evidence: This is an observation about the model's performance across different datasets.

claim: The rate-limiting step in coronavirus inactivation may not necessarily depend on the exact inactivating reactant.
source: This suggests that the rate-limiting step in coronavirus inactivation may not necessarily depend on the exact inactivating reactant.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation about the single activation energy.

claim: If inactivation depends on disruption of the virion once it has formed a complex with some inactivating reactant, the activation energy for that disruption event could depend mainly on the chemical properties of the virion itself.
source: We propose one simple potential mechanism for how this could be so: if inactivation depends on disruption of the virion once it has formed a complex with some inactivating reactant, the activation energy for that disruption event could depend mainly on the chemical properties of the virion itself (see Appendix, Interpretation of the single activation energy).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic explanation.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 strain HCoV-19 nCoV-WA1-2020 (MN985325.1) was used for this study.
source: We used SARS-CoV-2 strain HCoV-19 nCoV-WA1-2020 (MN985325.1; Holshue et al., 2020) for this study.
evidence: This describes the virus strain used in the experiments.

claim: Viable virus was quantified by end-point titration on Vero E6 cells.
source: We quantified viable virus by end-point titration on Vero E6 cells as described previously (Fischer et al., 2020; van Doremalen et al., 2020), and inferred posterior distributions for titers and exponential decay rates directly from raw titration data using Bayesian statistical models (see Statistical analyses and mathematical modeling, below).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: Virus stability was measured on polypropylene.
source: We measured virus stability on polypropylene (ePlastics, reference PRONAT.030X24X47S/M) as previously described (van Doremalen et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the experimental surface used.

claim: A solution of DMEM supplemented with 2 mM L-glutamine, 2% fetal bovine serum, and 100 units/mL penicillin/streptomycin, containing 105 TCID50/mL SARS-CoV-2 was prepared.
source: We prepared a solution of Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, a common cell culture medium) supplemented with 2 mM L-glutamine, 2% fetal bovine serum, and 100 units/mL penicillin/streptomycin, and containing 105 TCID50/mL SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This describes the experimental preparation.

claim: 50 μL aliquots of SARS-CoV-2 suspension were placed onto polypropylene disks.
source: We then placed 50 μL aliquots of this SARS-CoV-2 suspension onto the polypropylene disks under nine environmental conditions: three RH (40%, 65%, and 85%) at each of three temperatures (10°C, 22°C, and 27°C).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Controlled environmental conditions were produced in incubators with protection from UV-B or UV-C exposure.
source: These controlled environmental conditions were produced in incubators (MMM Group CLIMACELL and Caron model 6040) with protection from UV-B or UV-C exposure.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: 216 disks were prepared corresponding to three replicates per eight post-deposition time-points for the nine conditions.
